what-is-strike.title: What is Strike? A plain-English guide to the exchange
what-is-strike.subtitle: What you can trade on Strike, how copy trading works, who it is for, and how a first visit goes, in plain words for people who have never traded a perp.

faq.q: Do I need ADA or a Cardano wallet?
faq.a: No. An Ethereum or Solana wallet works too, and deposits can be made by card.
No. Stocks, indices and commodities trade on the same account as Bitcoin, as perps.

faq.q: Can I copy a trader instead of trading myself?
faq.a: Yes. Copy trading places a trade on your account whenever the trader you chose makes one, within limits you set.

what-is-strike.html:
What is Strike?

Strike Finance is a perpetual futures exchange. A perpetual future, or perp, is a contract that follows the price of something, such as Bitcoin or Tesla, without you owning it. You can profit if the price rises, by going long, or if it falls, by going short.

Strike started on Cardano in May 2025. It now runs its own trading engine with an order book, the system large exchanges use. Buyers and sellers post the prices they want, and the engine matches them. Your funds sit in smart contracts on the blockchain, and your balance is held in US dollars.

What can you trade?

Strike lists 34 markets. They fall into four groups.

TypeExamples
CryptoBitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, XRP, Cardano, HYPE
Stocks and private companiesNvidia, Tesla, Alphabet, Coinbase, SpaceX
IndicesS&P 500, Nasdaq-100
CommoditiesGold, silver, WTI crude oil

Everything sits on one account and one balance. You do not need a separate stock broker to trade Nvidia next to Bitcoin.

What is copy trading?

Copy trading lets Strike place trades on your account whenever a trader you choose makes a trade. You can copy traders on Strike, or any wallet on Hyperliquid, a large exchange where every trade is public. You choose how big each copied trade is, and you can cap how much of your balance it uses.

Who it's for

  • You trade crypto and want stocks or gold too. A Bitcoin trade and a gold trade can sit on the same account.
  • You would rather not pick every trade. You copy a trader whose record you have checked, with limits on how much of your balance each copy can use.
  • You are new to trading. Connect a wallet, deposit a small amount, and learn while the numbers are small. This series walks you through it.

How to get started

  1. Go to app.strikefinance.org in a browser, or use the Strike mobile app.
  2. Sign in by connecting a wallet. Wallets on Cardano, Ethereum and Solana all work.
  3. Deposit. Send crypto from a Cardano, Ethereum, Solana, Base, Arbitrum or Bitcoin wallet, or pay by card up to $50,000. Coins that move in price are swapped to dollars on arrival, so your balance is always in US dollars.
  4. Look around before you trade. The Trade page shows the chart and the order panel; Copy Trading and Earn have their own menus.

A worked example

This is an example, not a suggestion. Say you deposit $100 and open a $100 long on gold with no leverage. If gold rises 5%, your position is worth about $105, less a small trading fee. If gold falls 5%, it is worth about $95.

With leverage, both of those moves get bigger. That is the topic of the leverage guide, part 3 of this series.

Things worth knowing

  • Leverage can liquidate you. If a leveraged trade moves far enough against you, the exchange closes it and you lose the money behind it. Part 4 of this series explains how to keep clear of that.
  • Withdrawals have limits. Strike caps how much can leave in any rolling 1-hour and 24-hour window. If a withdrawal would go over the cap, it waits until earlier withdrawals age out of the window.
  • Copying a trader does not copy their results. Your copy uses your own leverage and size, and it starts from the moment you subscribe. Your results can differ from theirs.

How I use it

I do not trade by hand. I copy two traders from Hyperliquid on Strike, one on my main account and one on a sub-account. I check every trader's full history first. My rule: decide your limits before your first copy, not after your first loss.

what-is-a-perp.title: What is a perp? Perpetual futures explained in plain English
what-is-a-perp.subtitle: A perpetual future follows a price and never expires. What that means, how hourly funding keeps it close to the real price, and how to find a market on Strike.

faq.q: Do I own any Bitcoin when I buy a BTC perp?
faq.a: No. You hold a contract that follows Bitcoin's price, backed by the dollars in your Strike account.
It does not. A perp runs until you close it or it is closed for you, which part 4 of this series explains.

faq.q: Can I profit when prices fall?
faq.a: Yes. Going short on a perp earns when the price drops, and loses when it rises.

faq.q: Why is the perp's price slightly different from the real price?
faq.a: The perp trades on its own order book, so it drifts. Hourly funding pulls it back towards the index price.

toc.title: How to find a market on Strike

what-is-a-perp.html:
What is a perp?

A future is an agreement to trade something at a set price on a set date. A perpetual future, or perp, drops the date. The contract keeps running for as long as you hold it, and its price follows the asset it is named after.

On Strike, a BTC-USD perp follows the price of Bitcoin. If you think the price will rise, you go long: you profit as it climbs. If you think it will fall, you go short: you profit as it drops.

Either way you never hold any Bitcoin. Your position is a number on the exchange, backed by the dollars in your account.

What keeps the price honest?

Nothing forces a perp to match the asset on its own, so exchanges use funding. The exchange compares the perp's price with an index price, a reference built from the asset's price on other venues. When the perp trades above the index, longs pay shorts a small fee; when it trades below, shorts pay longs. On Strike, funding is settled every hour, on the hour.

The payments are tiny per hour. In Strike's own example, the rate is 0.00125% an hour. On a $100 position that is about a tenth of a cent, paid or received, every hour.

TermMeaning
LongYou profit when the price rises
ShortYou profit when the price falls
Index priceThe asset's price elsewhere, used as the reference
Mark priceThe price Strike uses to value your position
FundingHourly payment between longs and shorts

Who it's for

  • You want to trade a move, not hold the asset. No wallet for the coin, no broker for the share, no vault for the gold.
  • You want to be able to go short. A spot purchase only profits when prices rise. A perp lets you take the other side.
  • You want one account for different things. On Strike the same balance trades crypto, stocks, indices and commodities.

How to find a market on Strike

  1. Open app.strikefinance.org and sign in with your wallet.
  2. Click the market name at the top left of the Trade page, BTC-USD by default. A list opens.
  3. Use the tabs to narrow it: Crypto, TradFi for stocks, indices and commodities, and a search box for a name.
  4. Each row shows the last price, the 24-hour change, the volume and the funding rate on its 8-hour basis. Pick one and the chart and order panel switch to it.

A worked example

This is an example, not a suggestion. Say you open a $100 long on the BTC-USD perp with no leverage, and Bitcoin rises 5%. Your position is now worth about $105. Close it and you keep the $5, less a small trading fee on the way in and out.

If Bitcoin had fallen 5% instead, closing would leave you about $95.

A short works in reverse. Open a $100 short, and a 5% fall earns about $5 while a 5% rise loses about $5. Funding adds or takes a fraction of a cent an hour while the position is open.

Things worth knowing

  • Funding runs both ways. Depending on the market, you may pay or receive it. The list shows each market's 8-hour rate, and Strike settles one eighth of it every hour.
  • Fees are small but real. Strike's base fee for taking liquidity is 0.050% of the trade's value, and placing a resting order earns a 0.005% rebate.
  • Leverage changes everything. The examples above use none. With leverage a smaller move produces the same gain or loss, and a large enough move closes the trade. That is the next two guides.

long-short-leverage.title: Long, short and leverage: what 2x, 10x and 20x really mean
long-short-leverage.subtitle: Going long or short on Strike, what leverage really multiplies, how the same 5% move plays out at 2x, 10x and 20x, and the cross and isolated margin modes.

faq.q: Can I lose more than my margin?
faq.a: With isolated margin, the amount locked to that position is what is at risk. With cross margin the position can draw on your whole account balance.

faq.q: Is 1x leverage the same as buying the coin?
faq.a: Close, but not the same. You hold a contract that follows the price, you pay or receive hourly funding, and you never hold the coin itself.

faq.q: Which margin mode does Strike use if I do nothing?
faq.a: cross margin, set per market. You can switch any market to isolated from the order panel.

faq.q: Does changing leverage move my liquidation price?
faq.a: Yes. Higher leverage means less margin behind the same position, so the liquidation price sits closer to your entry.

toc.title: What long, short and leverage mean
How to set leverage and margin mode on Strike

long-short-leverage.html:
What long, short and leverage mean

Going long is buying a perp because you expect the price to rise. Going short is selling one you do not own, because you expect the price to fall. Both are a single click on Strike: the order panel has a Long/Buy side and a Short/Sell side.

Leverage is the ratio between the size of your position and the money you put behind it, called margin. With $100 of margin at 10x leverage you hold a $1,000 position. The exchange lends the rest, and your $100 absorbs the gains and losses on the whole $1,000. That is why the same price move feels ten times bigger.

The leverage box on Strike shows the setting for the market you are on. Each market has a cap, and it falls as positions grow. On Bitcoin the first tier allows up to 100x for positions up to $10,000; larger positions are capped lower.

Cross and isolated margin

Strike has two margin modes, set per market. Cross margin, the default, lets every cross position draw on your whole account balance as its buffer. Isolated margin locks a fixed amount to one position, so only that amount is at risk. Cross keeps your liquidation price further away; isolated caps what one bad trade can cost.

Who it's for

  • You want to make a small deposit go further. Leverage does that, and the next section shows what it costs when the price goes the other way.
  • You think a price will fall. A short earns when it does, something a plain purchase cannot do.
  • You run more than one position. Cross or isolated decides whether they share a buffer or stand alone.

How to set leverage and margin mode on Strike

  1. Open a market on the Trade page. The order panel sits on the right.
  2. The top row shows the margin mode, Cross or Isolated, and the leverage, for example 10x. Click either to change it.
  3. Set the leverage with the slider or by typing a number. Lowering leverage always works; raising it may be refused if your position is already in a higher tier.
  4. Pick Long/Buy or Short/Sell, enter a size, and the panel shows the margin it will take and the estimated liquidation price before you confirm.

A worked example

This is an example, not a suggestion. Say you put $100 behind a long on Bitcoin and the price moves 5%.

LeveragePosition sizePrice +5%Price −5%
1x$100+$5−$5
2x$200+$10−$10
10x$1,000+$50−$50
20x$2,000+$100−$100

At 20x the 5% drop costs the whole $100. In practice the exchange closes the position a little before that point, which is what the next guide is about. A short behaves the same way with the signs reversed.

Things worth knowing

  • Leverage does not change the odds. It changes how much each move is worth, both ways.
  • Fees scale with position size, not margin. Strike's base taker fee is 0.050% of the position's value, so a $1,000 position pays ten times the fee of a $100 one.
  • Funding scales the same way. The hourly funding payment is worked out on the full position.
  • Cross margin puts the whole account on the line. One losing position can draw down the balance that other positions rely on. Isolated margin stops that, at the cost of a closer liquidation price.

liquidation.title: Liquidation, and how to avoid it: a plain-English guide
liquidation.subtitle: What the liquidation price is, why leverage pulls it closer, how Strike closes a position in stages, and the habits that keep a first trade well clear of it.

faq.q: Will Strike warn me before liquidating?
faq.a: The liquidation price is shown next to the position at all times, and the margin ratio rises as you get close. The closing itself is automatic.

faq.q: Can I get the margin back after a liquidation?
faq.a: No. The margin behind the position covers the loss, and any surplus from a better fill goes to the backstop under the liquidation fee rules.

faq.q: Does a lower leverage setting cost anything?
faq.a: No. It means a smaller position for the same margin, so smaller gains and losses per move, and a liquidation price further away.

faq.q: What is the difference between a stop-loss and the liquidation price?
faq.a: A stop-loss is a price you choose, where Strike closes the trade for you. The liquidation price is where the exchange must close it to cover the loss, so the first belongs well before the second.

toc.title: How to check and move your liquidation price

liquidation.html:
What liquidation is

Every leveraged position has margin behind it. A move against you eats into that margin. Strike requires a minimum to stay in the trade, the maintenance margin: a small percentage of the position's value, 0.4% on a Bitcoin position of up to $10,000. When your remaining margin falls to that line, the position is liquidated: closed by the exchange, not by you.

The liquidation price is the price at which that happens. Strike shows it as an estimate in the order panel before you trade, and next to each open position afterwards. The margin ratio is the same idea as a percentage: maintenance margin divided by what you have left, where 100% means liquidation.

Why leverage moves it closer

At 2x, the price has to fall about halfway before your margin is gone. At 10x, about a tenth. At 20x, a 5% move is enough. Leverage does not change how far prices move, only how far they can move before you are out.

How Strike liquidates

Strike does not dump the whole position at once. A solvent position is reduced in stages, up to five attempts on the public order book, each sized to the current risk. If a reduction restores the account, the rest stays open.

Only a bankrupt position, or one still unsafe after the final attempt, goes to the backstop. A protocol vault takes it on, and as a last resort Strike trims positions on the profitable side, which it calls auto-deleveraging.

Who it's for

  • You are about to use leverage for the first time. The habits below are for you.
  • You already hold a position. The liquidation price next to it says how much room it has.
  • You copy a trader. Your copies use your leverage, so the liquidation prices are yours, not theirs.

How to check and move your liquidation price

  1. On the Trade page, set your size and leverage. The panel's Est. Liquidation Price updates as you change them.
  2. Lower the leverage and watch the estimate move away from the current price. That is the simplest lever you have.
  3. Tick TP/SL to attach a stop-loss: a price at which Strike closes the position for you, before the liquidation price.
  4. After you trade, the Positions table shows each liquidation price. Under isolated margin you can add margin to push it further away.

A worked example

This is an example, not a suggestion. Take the $100 long on Bitcoin from the last guide, at 10x, so a $1,000 position. If Bitcoin falls about 9.6%, the $100 of margin is almost gone and the maintenance margin line is crossed. Strike starts closing the position around there.

Now take the same $100 at 2x, a $200 position. The price has to fall close to 50% before the same thing happens. Each 1% move is worth $2 instead of $10, and the trade survives an ordinary bad week.

Things worth knowing

  • Liquidation is not free. On top of the lost margin, Strike can charge an adaptive liquidation fee when the forced close fills better than the bankruptcy price.
  • Cross and isolated behave differently. Under cross margin your whole balance is the buffer, so the price is further away but the whole account is exposed. Under isolated only the locked margin is at risk.
  • A stop order is not a guarantee. It becomes a market order when triggered, so in a fast market the fill can be worse than the stop price. It still acts long before the exchange has to.
  • Copied positions can be liquidated too. If a lead you copy is liquidated, your copy closes by the same fraction. Your own copy can also be liquidated on its own, at your leverage.

How I use it

I only hold copied positions. Before any copy starts, I lock the leverage on every market the lead trades and cap how much of the account a copy can use. I check the liquidation prices after every new position, not only when the market turns.
